answer.label: Not Eleanor Roosevelt — an anonymous modern saying
answer.authorDates: Origin unknown · full saying first documented June 1993
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator traced this saying and found no substantive evidence that Eleanor Roosevelt ever said or wrote it; the earliest attribution to her that QI located is a 1999 Usenet post, long after her death in 1962. The line is a stitched-together modern proverb: the “history / mystery” rhyme and the “gift / present” pun evolved separately for decades before being combined, and the earliest full version QI documents is a June 1993 graduation speech at Rutgers Preparatory School, where the speaker credited only “a former journalist.” The creator remains anonymous.
answer.confidenceText: No evidence in Roosevelt’s writings; the earliest documented full version credits an unnamed journalist.

source.excerpt: Yesterday is history. Tomorrow is a mystery. But today is a gift, and that is why it’s called the present.
trail: 1855 – c.1939, the rhyme alone. Quote Investigator ↗ documents the history/mystery pairing in an 1855 Christmas verse, an Emily Dickinson poem of around 1873 (“Yesterday is history / ‘Tis so far away… Yesterday is mystery”), a 1910 newspaper line, and a 1939 tailor’s message to graduates. No gift, no present.
1991, the pun alone. Liz Curtis Higgs uses “Every day is a gift, that’s why we call it the present,” crediting an anonymous source — per QI ↗.

June 1993, the halves join. The earliest full expression QI locates, in a New Jersey graduation speech, credited to an unnamed former journalist. A Family Circus panel of 31 August 1994 runs a close variant. See the citations ↗.

1999, Roosevelt’s name appears. A Usenet post is the earliest Roosevelt ascription QI found; Wikiquote ↗ keeps the line in its Disputed section because no book crediting her cites an original reference.

2008, the wording goes global. Master Oogway delivers the line in Kung Fu Panda, framing it as “a saying” — see Wikiquote: Kung Fu Panda ↗. The QI chronology does not cover the film; it is the populariser, not a source.
source.excerptNote: The wording of the earliest full version Quote Investigator documents, from June 1993. The speaker attributed it to an unnamed former journalist, not to Eleanor Roosevelt.
source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted. The saying has no identified author and no identified first publication — Quote Investigator concludes the creator is anonymous and the earliest documented full version is a 1993 spoken address. Because the origin is unknown, quotle.info makes no public-domain claim; specific later renderings (the 1994 Family Circus panel, the 2008 Kung Fu Panda screenplay) are separately protected works owned by their publishers and studios.

author.name: Eleanor Roosevelt
author.heading: About Eleanor Roosevelt
author.metaLine: 1884–1962 · U.S. First Lady, diplomat & human-rights advocate
author.bio: Eleanor Roosevelt was the longest-serving First Lady of the United States, from 1933 to 1945, and afterwards a United Nations delegate who chaired the drafting of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. She was a prolific writer — a daily newspaper column, several memoirs, and an enormous correspondence — which is precisely why the absence of this line from her documented work matters. She is the credited name here, not the source: the saying is an anonymous twentieth-century proverb that only became attached to her decades after she died.

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit, and why it’s wrong
misattribution.intro: Four names get attached to this line, in different ways — two people are genuinely credited with it, one is a film character who popularised it, and one used only half of it while crediting an anonymous source. None of the attributions holds up.

items.why: Quote Investigator located no substantive evidence ↗ for the ascription, and dates the earliest attribution to her to a 1999 Usenet message — she died in 1962. Wikiquote files it under Disputed ↗, noting that the books crediting her cite no original reference.

Goodreads credits the line to Bil Keane ↗ (QI renders the name “Bill Keane”; the cartoonist spelled it Bil). QI does document a Family Circus panel of 31 August 1994, but its wording is different — “Yesterday’s the past, tomorrow’s the future, but today is a GIFT. That’s why it’s called the present” — and it postdates the June 1993 full version ↗.

The film has Oogway say “Yesterday is history, tomorrow is a mystery, but today is a gift. That’s why it is called the present ↗” — and explicitly frames it as “a saying,” which by 2008 it plainly was. Millions first met the line here; nobody invented it here.
QI’s 1991 citation ↗ has Higgs using “Every day is a gift, that’s why we call it the present” while crediting an anonymous source — so even the pun was already in circulation.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer is that nobody owns this line. The earliest documented full version, in June 1993 ↗, was itself credited to an unnamed “former journalist,” and Quote Investigator concludes the creator remains anonymous — while allowing that earlier examples may still be found.

context.heading: A proverb assembled from spare parts
lead: Most fake quotes are a real line pinned to the wrong mouth. This one is stranger: it is a saying that grew, piece by piece, out of ordinary newspaper English. Quote Investigator’s chronology shows the “history / mystery” rhyme circulating on its own from the mid-nineteenth century — an 1855 Christmas verse in The Daily Post, a 1910 line in The Courier-Journal, a 1939 tailor’s message to graduates reading “Yesterday is History — Tomorrow, a Mystery — But Today is NOW AND TODAY IS YOURS!”

The “gift / present” pun is a separate invention, documented by QI in 1991 in the work of Liz Curtis Higgs, who herself credited an anonymous source. The two halves are welded together in the earliest full version QI found: a June 1993 graduation speech in New Jersey. A Family Circus panel ran a close cousin in August 1994, and the line reached global saturation in 2008 when Master Oogway delivered it in Kung Fu Panda. Eleanor Roosevelt’s name only enters the record in 1999.
detailsBody: Emily Dickinson is sometimes dragged in as an ancestor, and QI does document a poem of hers from around 1873 beginning “Yesterday is history / ‘Tis so far away” and continuing “Yesterday is mystery.” It is a genuine antecedent for the rhyme, not a source for the modern proverb — there is no gift, and no present.

QI is explicit that its 1993 citation may not be the end of the story: it suspects earlier examples of the full saying exist and may yet be found. That honest hedge is worth keeping. What is settled is the negative finding: nothing links the line to Eleanor Roosevelt.
context.pull: The two halves of this saying spent a century apart before anyone joined them.
